Moderator: 
Ladies and gentlemen, good day, and welcome to Timken India Q2 FY27 Earnings Conference 
Call hosted by Avendus. As a reminder, all participant lines will be in the listen-only mode and 
there will be an opportunity for you to ask questions after the presentation concludes. Should 
you need assistance during the conference call, please signal an operator by pressing star then 
zero on your touchtone phone. Please note that this conference is being recorded.  
I now hand the conference over to Mr. Krupashankar. Thank you, and over to you, sir. 
Krupashankar: 
Good evening. I appreciate everyone joining in for the 2Q FY27 Conference Call of Timken 
India Limited. We have with us Mr. Sanjay Koul, Chairman and Managing Director; and Mr. 
Sujit Kumar Pattanaik, the CFO of the company. 
I'll now hand over the call to them, and over to you, sir, for opening remarks. 
Sanjay Koul: 
Thank you so much. Thank you very much, Krupaji. So formally, good afternoon, and thanks a 
lot for joining this conference call today. I formally welcome you to the Timken India Investor 
call to discuss the financial results for the second quarter and also half year ended September 
30, 2026. So when we entered the FY27, it was on a positive note, as you know, and I am pleased 
to report that the momentum has continued into the second quarter as well. 
 
During Q2, we delivered, I think, a strong double-digit revenue growth accompanied by a nice 
little growth in profitability. The performance reflects continued demand across all the key end 
markets and a little bit delay in the rail, the contribution from our expanded capacity and the 
disciplined execution across both domestic and export businesses. Update on this Q2 FY26 - 27 
standalone. 
Revenue from operations stood at INR 969 crores, representing a growth of 25.4% over the 
corresponding quarter last year. So quarter compared to the last year was 25%. Revenue also 
grew almost 4.3% over Q1 '27. PBT for the quarter stood at INR 156 crores compared to INR 
120 crores in Q2 '26, representing a growth of almost 29.5%. PBT margin for the quarter stood 
at 16.1% compared with 15.6% in the corresponding quarter last year. So that is a 50 basis point 
improvement. 
Net profit after tax for the quarter stood at INR 116 crores compared with INR 89 crores in Q2, 
representing a nice growth of 29.7%. EBITDA margin for the quarter is at approximately 19.2%. 
So I think improvement in profitability is encouraging for the company. And obviously, there 
are cost pressures that is in the background. We have new vessels. So depreciation is there. Cost 
of fuel has gone up. Gas has gone up. And against that, this is pretty encouraging. 
 
So quickly on the half year performance. For the first half of FY27 stand-alone, revenue from 
operations stood at INR 18,984 million an increase of almost 20% year-on-profit. Profit before 
tax was almost INR 306 crores, while profit after tax at INR 231 crores, so an increase of 19%. 
Quickly on the consolidated numbers, the quarter stood at INR986 crores compared to INR 786 
crores in Q2 FY26. PBT was INR 162 crores while profit after tax was INR 120 crores, an 
approximately increase of 29% Y-o-Y. For the first half of FY27, the consolidated revenues are 
INR 1,929 crores, while consolidated net profit after tax stood at INR 240 crores. 

 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
     
 
Timken India Limited 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
October 30, 2026 
 
Page 3 of 10 
 
 
So overall, new Bharuch facility continues to progress through its ramp-up phase with the lines 
capitalized, we are focused on improving utilization. I'm sure that would be a question, but we 
are progressing on that. We are increasing the utilization. Our investment towards rail expansion 
at Jamshedpur and plain bearing at Bharuch, they are on target. 
So very soon, we should be able to commission and start the PPAPs and things like that. Also, 
the amalgamation of Timken GGB Technology Private Limited with Timken India Limited is 
progressing smoothly. So that regulatory process is on. So the proposed integration is aimed at 
driving obviously, synergies, efficiencies and simplifying the overall structure. 
 
On the cost side, cost is going up. So that is a focus area. So we are working on cost reduction, 
etcetera. So as you know, that cost is going to be a challenge in coming months and years also. 
The external environment remains mixed. Global industry activity continues to be influenced by 
geopolitics. So that is a challenge, as we all know, trade-related uncertainties are very much 
there and supply chain alignments are happening with every passing week. 
So we are connected to our customers. At the same time, demand from our key customer segment 
is okay. We continue to monitor development. So I would say that domestically, we should be 
pretty much okay as the demand looks to very  solid. Execution remains the key. So I would say 
that overall, it is a fairly nice picture as we walk into the next quarter as well.  
With that, I would throw the line open for questions, please. 
Moderator: 
Thank you very much. we will now begin with the question-and-answer session. The first 
question is from the line of Raghunandhan NL from Nuvama Research Private Limited.Please 
go ahead. 
Raghunandhan NL: 
Thank you sir for the opportunity. Congratulations on the strong all-round performance. Sir, can 
you please share the segment-wise revenue for Q2, which you generally do? 
Sanjay Koul: 
Yes, sure, why not. So yes, so on the front-end wise unit, Q2 FY27, rail was at INR156.7 crores. 
So that was 16% of the pie. Mobile others was INR204 crores. That was 21% of the pie. 
Distribution remained at INR148.8 crores, which was 15% of the pie. Process stood at INR190.9 
crores, which was 20% of the pie and exports was at INR262.7 crores, which was 27%. And 
then we have some export incentives. So that is how the Q2 INR969.3 crores spread out. 
Raghunandhan NL: 
Noted, sir. Thank you so much for that. And with regards to Bharuch plant, can you indicate 
how was the revenue utilization for Q2? How do you see the ramp-up going ahead? Have we 
reached 70% as of now, which was earlier target for September? 
Sanjay Koul: 
Yes. So the work is in full bloom and the capacity utilization is not yet at 70% but the 
certification, MOCs, because they were served from different plants. So MOCs are dependent 
on the sales side, which is the customer side, we are roughly at -- Sujit, currently at what? 
Sujit Kumar Pattanaik: 
Yes. So overall plant, if we look at it, we are anywhere close to, I would say, 60%... 
Sanjay Koul.: 
60% 

 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
     
 
Timken India Limited 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
October 30, 2026 
 
Page 4 of 10 
 
Sujit Kumar Pattanaik: 
But if you look at it, specifically the SRB plant, which the Chairman told in the last meeting, 
where the capacity is slightly higher than our CRB lines. So SRB lines, we have already reached 
70% for the quarter, what we promised in the last quarter. CRB lines are still below 60%, I would 
say. So on an average, it is at 60%. And from a revenue perspective for this quarter was very 
close to INR75 crores. 
Raghunandhan NL: 
Noted, sir. That's a good improvement compared to Q1 and Q3 should be much better.  
Sanjay Koul: 
Yes SRB -- the SRB lines are getting more traction. 
Raghunandhan NL: 
Got it, sir. And sir, exports has seen a very strong growth of 60% Y-o-Y and 30% Q-o-Q. Can 
you indicate how is the traction? Which regions would U.S. be the key driver of growth? And 
how do you see the momentum continuing? 
Sanjay Koul: 
And the momentum is going to be pretty healthy in quarters to come for sure. And very soon, 
with North American rail market also Timken Company, they are getting aligned to the buying 
behavior of those customers, I think more better days in terms of export are going to be there. 
That rail piece would have more traction in quarters, it won't be immediate. Quarters to come, 
but overall on bearings, it is going to be pretty healthy. 
Raghunandhan NL: 
Good to hear that, sir. Just a last question. On the cost inflation, can you indicate how much was 
the impact in Q2? And we can see that raw material cost Q-o-Q has gone up 130 basis points as 
a percentage of revenue and other costs like gas -- fuel, gas has also gone up. Would the entire 
cost be passed on to customers? Would there be some negotiation? Would there be some 
absorption expected, especially with the non-auto customers? 
Sanjay Koul: 
So I'll ask Sujit to reply, but generally, the cost is going up and will still go up and nobody can 
absorb it. Industry -- bearing industry cannot absorb it. They might absorb it for a quarter or so, 
but overall, they have to pass it on. So the endeavor is actually to pass it on. That is the job of 
the sales people in the bearing industry because this is not a onetime cost or a small cost. 
Carbides have gone 200% up. Steel is going up and then your gases have already gone up. Then 
if you look at the labor, labor is going up. So you name the area, the cost is going up and going 
on the up. And you can only do that much CI improvement. So it has to be passed on. 
 
Our endeavor is to pass it on, and we'll continuously work on that. Both auto and non-auto, there 
is -- the industry cannot absorb it, not -- forget about Timken India. Everybody has to, for the 
sake of survival, pass it on. And our major customers understand it. They are passing on. But 
automotive, they will kind of delay it a little bit here and there. Industry people, otherwise, on 
the industrial side is coming up. And over to Sujit for a little bit more mathematical equation. 
Sujit Kumar Pattanaik: 
Yes. Maybe just one additional point there, that 130 basis points, what we talked about, I think 
you talked about that gross margin impact. So that's not necessarily entire thing is coming 
because of the input cost inflation. So you have a little bit of unfavorable mix also, which is 
playing the role there, basically the mix, the way you sell it in the front-end units. So there is a 
little bit of input cost inflation in there, which we are continuously working on to pass it over to 
the customers. 

 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
     
 
Timken India Limited 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
October 30, 2026 
 
Page 5 of 10 
 
You will always have a timing gap cost and price difference. But there is also an unfavorable 
mix there, which is playing a role. So probably I would say 50% is because of unfavorable mix 
and 50% is because of input cost difference between price and cost timing difference. 
Raghunandhan NL: 
That is very helpful, sir. Just a clarification, unfavorable mix refers to lower share of railway 
and distribution. 
Sanjay Koul: 
Yeah, rail was low in the quarter. That is the unfavorable mix because the global -- the rail tender 
was delayed. 
Raghunandhan NL: 
Thank you so much. I follow back to the queue.  
Moderator: 
Thank you. The next question is from the line of Varun Jain from Dolat Capital Private Limited. 
Please go ahead.  
Varun Jain: 
Hi Sir, Good evening. So I have a couple of questions. So first question is, sir, in this quarter, 
your depreciation declined to INR289 million from INR314 million in Q1, while your capital 
work in progress increased almost -- it almost doubled. So why is that? 
Sanjay Koul: 
Very good question. If I had a Nobel Prize for a question, I would give it to you. So Sujit... 
Sujit Kumar Pattanaik: 
Yes. So that depreciation is a little bit of accounting noise, I would say, the reclassification 
between last quarter and current quarter between other expense and depreciation, which has been 
trued off in this quarter. So there is no structural reduction in depreciation. It was more of an 
accounting reclassification from other expense depreciation, very close to INR1.3 crores. 
Varun Jain: 
Okay. Got it, sir. And sir, the other questions were on Bharuch. So what was the Bharuch revenue 
in this quarter? And what are the margins we are realizing on CRB and SRB versus what we get 
on TRBs? 
Sujit Kumar Pattanaik: 
So INR75 crores -- so in terms of revenue is INR75 crores. We don't disclose separate margin 
at the plant level. We don't monitor that. It still one segment. From a revenue perspective, it is 
INR75 crores. The plant is ramping up. So as you know, kind of as we occupy and the capacity 
utilization improves quarter-over-quarter, that's definitely going to improve the margin. 
Sanjay Koul: 
But just generally, the SRB, CRB generally go to the industrial segment. Industrial segment is 
always better than the automotive segment in terms of holistic margin behavior. 
Varun Jain: 
Yes, sir, I understand. Like I directionally understand that they are higher margin, but is the 
difference like 300, 500 bps or more than that also? 
Sanjay Koul: 
That obviously, we don't state. So I will just tell you directionally. 
Varun Jain: 
Sure, sir. Sure.  
Sanjay Koul: 
Yeah, go ahead. Sorry, we lost you. 

 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
     
 
Timken India Limited 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
October 30, 2026 
 
Page 6 of 10 
 
Varun Jain: 
Yes, sir, my question -- other question was that this railway expansion of INR120 crores, is it 
still expected to start commercial production by December? And secondly, on this, that there 
were railway tenders which were delayed. So now have they started converting into orders? 
Sanjay Koul: 
So the new line would start getting into the trial runs in November and December only, then the 
PPAPs would start and then we'll qualify those lines. So that is all online as per the target. And 
as far as tender is concerned, so tender was delayed and the tender hopefully should get into in 
terms of -- because committee has not been set yet, committee will be set and all that stuff will 
happen in the next 2, 3 weeks. 
But in the meantime, there is some interim orders which are placed on wagon builders. So now 
the movement and traction on wagons and the tender is pretty much in full swing. So another 3 
weeks of tenders, those things will materialize into orders. 
Varun Jain: 
Okay, sir. Got it. And just the last... 
Moderator: 
Sorry to interrupt, Mr. Jain. I request that you to follow back the queue for follow-up questions. 
The next question is from the line of Rishi Vora from Kotak Securities Private Limited. 
Rishi Vora: 
My first question is just regarding SRB and CRB. While you said that INR75 crores was the 
quarterly contribution, like what would be the mix between the domestic and the export in this 
business? 
Sanjay Koul: 
Currently, it is heavily towards exports. And the domestic endeavor is on because those PPAPs 
and other things are happening. But this quarter sales is more tilted towards intercompany, which 
is exports. 
Rishi Vora: 
Understood. And sir, how should we think about, let's say, year-end utilization levels? Should it 
reach 80% - 85% by end of this financial year... 
Sanjay Koul: 
Yes. When we talk on the last quarter, when we have the investor call after the last quarter of 
the financial is over, so currently, CRBs are at roughly 50% to 60%, SRB is 70%. I would say 
overall, would be between 70% to 75%. 
Rishi Vora: 
Okay. Understood. And sir, just in terms of, obviously, you said that industrial generally makes 
better margins. How -- when this reaches a certain utilization levels, will the margin overall be 
accretive to our business? Or will it also depend on the domestic and the export mix at that point 
in time? I'm assuming that export would be accretive at this point in time as compared to 
domestic. 
Sanjay Koul: 
So directionally, industrial is always better than the automotive. And as we reach that critical 
mass, you will see a positive effect. Now how much all that time will tell us, but overall would 
be positive. Sujit, any comments? 
Sujit Kumar Pattanaik: 
But just one additional comment there for the last quarter, which is quarter 3 of the financial 
year... 
Moderator: 
Sorry to interrupt, sir. You sound very distant from the line. 

 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
     
 
Timken India Limited 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
October 30, 2026 
 
Page 7 of 10 
 
Sujit Kumar Pattanaik: 
No, I was just telling probably... 
Sanjay Koul: 
One minute you can come this side. Minute, one minute. Sujit is coming closer to the phone. 
Sujit Kumar Pattanaik: 
I was telling just one additional point. Since quarter 3 of the financial year, we have the year-
end as well. So generally, the seasonality for the last quarter of the calendar year is always a 
little bit of softening because of the export and the year end of December, so on and so forth. So 
that has to be considered as well by calculating the capacity utilization on the segment. 
Rishi Vora: 
Understood. And sir, just second question on the Process Industries ex CRB, SRB. Like can you 
just give some color on which segments during the quarter did well? And what's the outlook in 
some of the key segments within Process Industries? 
Sanjay Koul: 
Within processing wind is doing well. 
Rishi Vora: 
Sorry, sir? 
Sanjay Koul: 
Wind, wind. 
Rishi Vora: 
Okay. And like how should we think about the growth rates going forward for this business, 
excluding CRB, SRB? 
Sanjay Koul: 
Yes, it will be pretty stable. It is in a very nice spot currently. The Chinese and others are moving 
a lot of production of the gearboxes into India, and we are in a nice spot there. 
Moderator: 
The next question is from the line of Ashish from Leo Capital Limited. Please go ahead.  
Ashish: 
Congratulations on a good set of numbers. I have 2 questions. The first question would be, how 
is the overall global demand environment for various parts of the bearing business? Is demand 
likely to continue to be strong over the next few years? And which segments are seeing 
maximum demand momentum? That would be my first question. 
Sanjay Koul: 
So one is that the domestic demand is going to remain robust. You know GDP is at 7%. 
Infrastructure still is in full swing. Steel, I think last quarter was a little bit down the steel 
production. But overall, I would say that the domestic demand in coming years is going to be 
pretty much good. Now geopolitics is there. So nobody can predict that, what is going to have 
the impact of those things. But otherwise, the American market is also pretty much in a nice spot 
there. 
 
For us, the good attractive market in months and years to come, both domestically export would 
be rail for sure, and then the heavy truck segment across the board. Also, the off-highway 
segment is behaving well globally and also in India. So I would say that the demand looks 
globally. 
Obviously, Indian GDP is 7%, U.S. would be 2%, their base is huge. All that is very much there. 
The ASEAN is at 4% GDP growth and all that stuff. So I would say that domestic demand would 
be the king maker. But overall, bad days of exports, I think, are slowly getting over. 

 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
     
 
Timken India Limited 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
October 30, 2026 
 
Page 8 of 10 
 
Ashish: 
Got it. And secondly, how does the cost of production compare the Indian operation versus some 
of the global manufacturing in Europe and other parts of the world, is India meaningfully cost 
competitive? 
Sanjay Koul: 
Yes. Short answer, yes. 
Ashish: 
By how much? Would that be quantifiable? 
Sanjay Koul: 
No. It is in a good spot, I can tell you with a lot of confidence. And you should also look -- not 
for Timken India, in general, you should look at not only cost, you have to look at the capability, 
cost and delivery in one space when you do global export business. So it is not only the cost. 
You can have the best cost, but then you have the worst quality. You have the best cost, but your 
delivery is not right. So all that has to be seen in one. So that way, India scores over many, many 
countries. 
Moderator: 
The next question is from the line of Rakesh from Axis Asset Management Company. Please go 
ahead.  
Rakesh: 
Firstly, congratulations to execute the kind of profitability in this environment. First question is 
on the wind business, fairly new business, which we have been executing now. I mean, if you 
can elaborate how to think about our market share for the wind business either in domestic or 
the export market going forward? And where do you think you can -- what kind of capacity 
expansion would you require maybe 3 years out? 
Sanjay Koul: 
So on the wind business, this wind, especially the domestic wind consumption was very 
sluggish. So all the ZFs and the Flenders of the world were making gearboxes mostly for export. 
The good news is that now the domestic wind market is also picking up and domestic Indian 
wind companies are also picking up. 
So this market is going to be pretty much relevant in India for some more years, given the fact 
that we want to reduce the -- converting electricity through thermal that has to be reduced. And 
the need of the power is only going to go up and up and up as you see the data centers coming 
up and the rest of the stuff coming up, so the need of power is going to go up.  
And the need to have clean energy is also going up, which is no rocket science. So the local wind 
market for local production and consumption is going to go up. So that is pretty much okay. And 
Timken India Limited does not make the wind bearings. We buy from the sister concerns and 
sister concerns are investing in large sizes domestically. 
Rakesh: 
Okay. So I mean, could you double-click on that and tell us what segment or subsegment are we 
addressing today? And where I'm coming from is your -- one of your competitors recently made 
a comment where they are going very selective on the market they are choosing for the wind 
due to a lot of low-margin business going on... 
Sanjay Koul: 
So yes, yes, so that is the -- whoever has made the comment has made a valid comment. So we 
are also into the gearboxes and not on the main shaft generally. If we make money on the main 

 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
     
 
Timken India Limited 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
October 30, 2026 
 
Page 9 of 10 
 
shaft, then we go after it, that is a little bit commoditized. But the gearbox is what we've always 
been serving and we'll keep on serving. 
Rakesh: 
And any plans to localize this bearing in the future? 
Sanjay Koul: 
So Timken India Limited is not localizing it. But the other Timken entity in India is localizing 
it, and they are already producing it to certain size range, and we are further doing stuff on that, 
and we are buying and selling. Okay. We can take the last question. We got 2 minutes left. Any 
last question, please? 
Moderator: 
Yes, sir. The last question is from the line of Nikhil from ithoughtPMS. Please go ahead.  
Nikhil: 
So I have a couple of questions. First is on wind turbine upsizing. So Indian OEMs are moving 
away from 2-3-megawatt to 4-5-megawatt platforms. So at these sizes, gearbox makers are using 
hydrodynamic plane bearings instead of roller bearings. And they are also -- many of them are 
making them in-house, I believe. So how is Timken's bearing content per megawatt changing as 
these turbines increase in size? And are you seeing any substitution of your TRBs or CRBs in 
gearboxes made in India? 
Sanjay Koul: 
Yes. So on this wind, so obviously, India used to be a sub-megawatt market, then they started 
making 3 megawatts, there is no 4 megawatt in India, but 5 megawatt is coming into picture. 
And globally, it has gone even up to 14 - 15 megawatts. 8 megawatt is also pretty common. But 
India, I think 3 and 5 is going to be a common one for a long, long time. 
On the gearbox, there are many stages on the initial stage where your need on the bearing is 
lower is a plain bearing. So now plain bearing can be made out of brass, which is like a sleeve 
and has no technology in it. But if you have a technology where alternate material can be made, 
which is called Generation 3, Generation 4 and Timken has a company called GGB, which is 
pretty much heavily investing in the research for this in global arena. 
And that market is what can become a little bit different than the current plain bearing, which is 
nothing but a sleeve does not give you the optimal results out of the gearbox. But when you go 
beyond the -- when you go to the carrier bearings, taper rollers cannot be replaced as per the 
current technology available. And then as they become 5- and 6-megawatt bigger gearboxes, 
bigger, larger taper roller bearings will be needed and the lower stage might be and is being done 
plain bearings. 
As you know, one of the listed companies who are doing cage is doing plain bearings and some 
of the wind, as you rightly said, are doing the plain stuff themselves. But then there is a 
technology intervention into that in which hopefully, companies like Timken India Limited 
would be able to sell through alternate. 
But currently, we are concentrating on the upstage up carrier -- carrier tapers, which is pretty 
much going to stay. The plain bearing at the lower stage is a sleeve, was a taper roller bearing 
before, has become a sleeve and can become in future a Gen 3 alternate stuff into that. So there 
is further opportunity in that. 

 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
     
 
Timken India Limited 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
October 30, 2026 
 
Page 10 of 10 
 
Nikhil: 
Okay, okay. Thanks for such a detailed answer. That was very helpful. So just one more question. 
So has GGB currently won or qualified any orders in this space? 
Sanjay Koul: 
No. We have not yet capitalized. The machines are here. We still have to run them, and we are 
in the process of doing that. But we are already winning orders and supplying from our overseas 
by brand. We are buying from them, our GGB brand. But very soon, it will be produced here. 
So there will be a combination of selling imported product of GGB and produced in India at our 
Bharuch facility. 
Nikhil: 
Okay. And what kind of share do you expect from the wind sector versus distribution and process 
once like Bharuch reaches full utilization? 
Sanjay Koul: 
I did not understand the question. This is regarding? 
Nikhil: 
Once Bharuch reaches full utilization, how much of the overall revenue potential is going to be 
fulfilled by wind compared to your other... 
Sanjay Koul: 
Bharuch becomes overall. What would we... 
Sujit Kumar Pattanaik: 
Yes. So Bharuch, if you look at it -- if your question is specific to GGB today, I think if you look 
at it, our statement, I think very close to they're into INR70 crores, INR75 crores. And this 
Bharuch investments for GGB, what's going on for both FRC and metal polymer put together, I 
think INR35 crores, INR35 crores, INR70 crores of investments.  
And the asset turn is anywhere we do close to 1.5 to 2. So you can do the math. I think that is 
what the numbers will be coming out with the investment, which has been approved and 
undergoing as we speak. 
Moderator: 
Thank you. We take that as the last question for today. I now hand the conference over to the 
management for closing comments. 
Sujit Kumar Pattanaik: 
Thank you so much for joining us today. It's a pleasure hosting this call for quarter 2 of the 
financial year, and we will again catch up for the next quarter. Thank you. 
Moderator: 
Thank you. On behalf of Avendus, that concludes this conference. Thank you for joining us and 
you may now disconnect your line.
